newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Iraq's Aziz blames U.S. for aid distribution snags.
newsitem.headline: Iraq's Aziz blames U.S. for aid distribution snags.

text.p: Iraq's Deputy Prime Minister Tareq Aziz on Thursday said he complained to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan again about the delay in getting food and medical supplies to his country, saying the United States was at fault.
"I complained about the process of implementation," of an oil-for-food deal that allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months in order to buy food and medicine for its people.

The fund also earmarks monies for a reparation fund to compensate victims of Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait and pay for U.N. operations, headed by chief inspectors, Rolf Ekeus, seeking out Iraq's weapons of mass destruction.

"The oil has been sold," he said. "There is oil for the reparation fund, for expenses for Ekeus but not for food for the Iraqi people. There is an imbalance. It could be described as the "oil-for-nothing" deal," Aziz said.
He said he requested Annan "to expedite the process and let the Iraqi people benefit from this deal."

Aziz, who addresses the U.N. Earth Summit on the environment later on Thursday, said the U.N. teams supervising the food and medical distribution had no problems with the Iraqi authorities while the weapons inspectors said they did.

Aziz said he compared the two groups to Annan, implying that conflicts between weapons inspectors and Iraq were not Baghdad's fault, since both weapons inspectors and aid teams were dealing with Iraqi government officials.
"Why should there be a problem with U.N. officials on the other side," Aziz asked.

Comments by Aziz followed statements earlier Thursday by Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhhammad Rasheed, who said aid distribution under the oil deal had accelerated in recent weeks. Rasheed, speaking in Vienna where OPEC ministers had gathered, also reiterated that Iraq expected to resume oil sales in the next week to 10 days, delinking delayed aid distribution and the signing of oil contracts for fresh exports.

Iraq is allowed to sell $2 billion worth of crude under a humanitarian deal with United Nations. The so-called "oil-for-food" accord originally ran from December 10 to June 7, but was renewed for a further 180 days from June 8.
New oil sales have been delayed since that time until Iraq submits an aid distribution plan, and a pricing formula.
